Audio guide, stop nine. The room you are standing in was once the sorting hall of the harbour warehouse, and the beams above your head were cut from a single stand of Douglas fir in the years before the fire. Look at the iron wheels set into the floor; they carried crates along a track that ran the length of the building and out through the loading doors at the far end. Dockworkers called the track the snake, because it turned twice on its way to the water and because anyone who walked it in the dark was sure to stumble.

The crates came from every corner of the empire. Tea from Assam, coffee from the highlands of Jamaica, indigo, tallow, and bundles of dried hides that left a smell in the rafters for weeks after they had gone. Each crate was weighed at the door and chalked with a number, and the numbers were copied into ledgers by clerks who stood at a slanted desk near the window. Some of those ledgers survive, and if you lean close to the glass case you can still read the careful handwriting.

What the ledgers show is a town growing faster than its streets could follow. Census returns record the population rising from 4,200 in 1861 to 11,800-13,000 by 1890, with the steepest gains in the decades after the railway reached the quay. The piers were lengthened from 90 to 140 metres in the same period, and the old market square, which had once been the centre of everything, found itself at the edge of a city that no longer needed it. Families who had lived within sight of the water for generations moved inland, following the tram lines, while newcomers from the countryside took their places in the crowded terraces behind the warehouses.

By the time the harbour authority commissioned its own survey, the sorting hall was already obsolete. Container traffic demanded flat ground and long approaches, not a crooked track winding between stone walls, and the last cargo was lifted out through the loading doors in the spring of a year the guide will not name, because the exact date is disputed. The building stood empty for a decade. Rain came in through the roof, pigeons nested in the rafters, and the iron wheels rusted where they lay.

Restoration began in earnest after the council bought the site. Volunteers cleared twenty tonnes of rubble by hand, rebuilt the sluice that once kept the floor dry, and discovered beneath the flagstones a second track, narrower than the first, that no ledger mentions. The museum opened to the public in stages, one gallery at a time, and the last of the display cases was installed only recently. If you look through the doorway at the end of the hall, you can see the first of those cases now, lit from below, holding a single chalked crate lid. The number on it is the one we began with. Please continue to the next stop, where the tour turns to the men and women who worked this floor.
